title: A farmer in Jesus’ parable experienced what many people today would call the dream scenario.
paragraphs: A farmer in Jesus’ parable experienced what many people today would call the dream scenario.
His land produced an incredible harvest.
So much grain that his current barns could not contain it.

For most people, that would be the moment of celebration.
The moment when years of hard work finally paid off.
And in a sense, the harvest was a blessing.
But the danger began in what he said next.

Instead of lifting his eyes to heaven in gratitude…
He started talking to himself.
“What shall I do? I have no place to store my crops.”
Then he made a decision that seemed perfectly logical:
“I will tear down my barns and build bigger ones, and there I will store my surplus grain.”
Then he imagined his future.
“And I will say to myself, you have plenty of grain laid up for many years. Take life easy; eat, drink and be merry.”
From a human perspective, it sounded like wisdom.
From heaven’s perspective, it was spiritual blindness.
Because while the man was planning for decades…
God said he only had one night.

“You fool! This very night your life will be demanded from you.”
— Luke 12:20
Think about that moment.

This man had wealth.
He had success.
He had security.
But he didn’t have time.
And that is the lesson Jesus wanted everyone listening to understand.
The man’s problem wasn’t his harvest.
The Bible never condemns him for being productive or successful.
The real issue was his heart.
Notice something powerful in the story.
Five times he uses the words “I” and “my.”

My crops.
My barns.
My grain.
My goods.
My life.
God was never part of his equation.

No gratitude.
No generosity.
No thought about eternity.
Just accumulation.
Just expansion.
Just comfort.
And this is where the story quietly becomes uncomfortable for us today.
Because the rich fool is not just an ancient farmer.
He is a mirror.
Our culture constantly tells us the same story he believed.
Build bigger.
Earn more.
Store more.
Secure your future.
And while planning for the future is not wrong, Jesus warns about something deeper:
You can spend your whole life building bigger barns…
while ignoring the condition of your soul.
You can grow your business…
while shrinking your devotion.
You can increase your possessions…
while decreasing your dependence on God.
You can become financially rich…
while becoming spiritually empty.
The tragedy of the rich fool is not that he had wealth.
The tragedy is that he thought wealth meant security.
But the truth is something many people avoid thinking about:
Every barn we build will one day be left behind.
Every account.
Every investment.
Every possession.
None of it crosses eternity with us.
That is why Jesus ended the parable with a powerful warning:

“This is how it will be with whoever stores up things for themselves but is not rich toward God.”
— Luke 12:21
Being rich toward God looks very different from building bigger barns.
It looks like gratitude instead of entitlement.
It looks like generosity instead of hoarding.
It looks like trusting God instead of trusting wealth.
It looks like remembering that our life on earth is temporary, but our soul is eternal.
The rich fool thought his greatest problem was not having enough space for his harvest.
But his real problem was not having space for God in his plans.
And that question quietly comes to all of us today:
Are we building barns…
or building treasure in heaven?
Because one day, every one of us will stand before God.
And in that moment, the only wealth that will matter…
is whether we were rich toward Him.
If this message challenged you, share it so someone else can reflect on it too.
Sometimes the most loving warning is the one that reminds us:

Life is fragile.
Eternity is real.
And the soul is priceless.
What do you think Jesus meant by being “rich toward God”?
